investigation.v: Identify failing pod state

Anti-Pattern: Deploying 'latest' tags

answer: I'd halt the pipeline and check pod status via kubectl get pods.
Based on status, use describe pod for k8s events or kubectl logs for app crashes.
Execute kubectl rollout undo to immediately restore service.
Debug the root cause offline.

Run plan review to identify manual cloud changes

data.resolutionPerm: Import manual changes to state, resolve drift

practices.text: Best Practice: Plan review gating in Prod
Risk: Manual 'ClickOps' in Production

answer: First, I review pipeline logs to check if it's a state lock or a drift error.
If state lock, verify no other pipelines are running, then safely break the lock.
If drift, review the plan to see what was manually changed.
Either revert manual change, or import it into state.
recall: IaC is single source of truth

data.detection: Synthetic monitoring & Load Balancer health probes failed.

data.resolutionPerm: Implement Blue/Green or Canary deployment strategy

practices.text: Lesson: Always decouple deployments from releases
Prevention: Automated health checks before traffic switch

answer: My priority is MTTR. I immediately trigger a traffic switch back to the stable environment.
Once mitigated, verify why deployment strategy (e.g., Canary) didn't catch it.
Review logs to find if it was config, DB schema, or code issue.
Implement stricter health-probe gates.

data.reqs: Identify anomalous spend and optimize Compute, Storage, Logs, Networking.

Focus on the big four: Compute, Storage, Logs, and Networking.

Long-term, enforce strict tagging policies and buy Reserved Instances.

data.resolutionPerm: Ensure Private Endpoint lifecycle is automated via IaC

practices.text: Best Practice: Use Private Endpoints
Anti-Pattern: Opening SQL firewall to 'Allow All Azure Services'

answer: I'd use Kudu console to run 'tcpping' to the SQL IP and 'nameresolver' for hostname.
If IP fails, I check VNet routing and NSGs blocking 1433.
If hostname fails, verify the Private DNS Zone is linked to the VNet.
Resolve the missing link, then automate it in Terraform.

data.impact: High latency under load, app crashing (OOM).

investigation.v: Check target utilization metrics
Verify metrics-server pod is running

answer: First check `kubectl get hpa`. If <unknown>, Metrics Server is down or Resource Requests are missing.
HPA cannot calculate percentage utilization without a baseline request.
If pods are 'Pending', Cluster Autoscaler hit max limit.
Add requests to YAML and increase node limit.
recall: Pending Pods = Out of Nodes (CA issue)
HPA scales pods, CA scales nodes

data.reqs: Reduce build & deploy time to < 10 mins for developer feedback loop.

cost.v: Use Docker layer caching & npm/maven caching
Split unit, integration, and linting tests
Only build monorepo packages that changed

answer: A 40-minute pipeline destroys developer productivity. I would analyze the bottleneck stages.
First, implement dependency caching and Docker layer caching.
Refactor pipeline to run tests, linting, and scans as parallel jobs.
If it's a monorepo, implement incremental builds.

rca: Batch job run, cert expiry, or DB maintenance
data.resolutionImmediate: Mitigate issue (Failover to secondary region or restart)
data.resolutionPerm: Conduct Blameless RCA, implement automated fixes

practices.text: Lesson: Mitigate first, investigate root cause later
Prevention: Automate certificate renewals

answer: My first goal is detection and triage: what is broken and who is impacted?
I prioritize mitigation over finding the root cause—failing over or rolling back immediately.
Communication is key. Update status page every 30 mins.
Post-incident, lead a blameless RCA to find true root cause.

investigation.v: Identify exact stage of failure (Build, Deploy, DB)
Check if migrations are locked or partially applied
Check if old version is still serving traffic

rca: Bad artifact, missing config, or failed DB migration
data.resolutionImmediate: Trigger automated rollback to last known good state
data.resolutionPerm: Improve pre-flight checks and schema backwards compatibility

practices.text: Best Practice: Automated rollback triggers on failure
Risk: Manual intervention during active release window

answer: I would immediately check the pipeline logs to pinpoint the failure—was it code, config, or database?
If it impacted active users, I'd trigger the rollback strategy to restore the previous state.
Communicate the failed release to stakeholders and abort the window.
Investigate the RCA the next day without the pressure of the maintenance window.
recall: Never debug live in a release window

investigation.v: Did code/dependencies change?
Check node disk space and memory
Check if Service Principals/Tokens expired
Check for overnight auto-updates

rca: Out of disk space, expired secret, or transient network issue
data.resolutionImmediate: Clear workspace, restart agent, or update expired secret
data.resolutionPerm: Monitor agent disks, automate secret rotation, pin dependencies

practices.text: Best Practice: Wipe workspace before every build
Anti-Pattern: Auto-updating Jenkins plugins

answer: Since it worked yesterday, I look for environmental changes first.
I check if a secret expired, if the Jenkins Agent ran out of disk space, or if an upstream registry is down.
I'd also check if a developer introduced a new unpinned dependency.
I would clear the workspace and re-run. If it persists, isolate the exact failing step in the logs.

timeline.ev: Dev merges PR removing/renaming TF block

data.detection: Users report outage, monitoring shows missing endpoints.
rca: Terraform sees old resource as 'to be destroyed' and new as 'to be created'
Apply runs without human plan review
data.resolutionImmediate: Restore state from DB backups, re-run apply to recreate compute
data.resolutionPerm: Enforce Plan reviews, use prevent_destroy lifecycle hooks

practices.text: Prevention: Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to Databases
Prevention: Separate state files for App vs Data

answer: This is a severe incident. Immediate mitigation is recreating the compute resources via Terraform and restoring Databases from backups.
The root cause is usually a developer renaming a module, causing Terraform to destroy the old and create the new.
To prevent this, I would enforce mandatory Plan reviews in the pipeline for production.
I'd also add 'prevent_destroy = true' lifecycle hooks to all stateful resources.

title: Works Locally But Fails In Docker

data.impact: Deployment fails or app is unreachable inside cluster.

investigation.v: Check for missing dependencies or crash loops
Verify passed Environment Variables
Check if app binds to localhost instead of 0.0.0.0

rca: Missing host-level dependency, hardcoded 'localhost', or missing ENV
data.resolutionImmediate: Update code to bind to 0.0.0.0, pass correct ENVs
data.resolutionPerm: Use docker-compose for local dev to match target environment

practices.text: Best Practice: 12-Factor App methodology (Config in ENV)
Anti-Pattern: Hardcoding 'localhost' for DB connections

answer: The most common reason is networking. Apps binding to 'localhost' inside a container cannot be reached from the outside; they must bind to '0.0.0.0'.
Next, I'd check for missing Environment Variables or differences in the OS architecture.
I'd use 'docker logs' to see the exact crash, and 'docker exec' to check the filesystem.
Prevention is forcing developers to test locally using docker-compose.

data.errorState: Feature works in QA but throws 500s or timeouts in Prod
data.impact: Release rollback required, loss of trust.

investigation.v: Compare QA and Prod config maps / ENVs
Check if Prod DB lacks indexes needed for large tables
Check if Prod firewall blocks an external API

rca: Code passes functional tests in QA
Prod-specific issue (Scale, Missing Secret, Strict Firewall)
data.resolutionPerm: Use IaC to ensure strict environment parity. Implement Staging environment.

practices.text: Best Practice: Staging should be an exact replica of Prod (anonymized data)
Risk: Using different SKU tiers in QA vs Prod

answer: This happens due to a lack of Environment Parity. I look at three things: Config, Data, and Network.
Config: Prod might be missing a newly added secret or ENV var.
Data: The QA database might be tiny, so a missing index wasn't caught until it hit Prod scale.
Network: Prod firewalls (NSGs) are stricter and might block external API calls.
I'd rollback, fix the parity gap, and enforce IaC to keep environments synced.

data.impact: System degraded. High latency for end users.
rca: Unexpected batch job, crawler bot, or unoptimized DB query runs
data.resolutionImmediate: Manually scale up/out, block bad IPs, or restart pods

practices.text: Best Practice: Alerts should be actionable, not just informational
Prevention: Set up auto-scaling rules before manual alerts

answer: First, I acknowledge the alert and open the Grafana dashboard to confirm the CPU spike isn't a false positive.
I check logs to see what's driving the CPU—is it a traffic spike, a rogue bot, or a heavy scheduled batch job?
To mitigate, I'd manually scale out the replicas (if auto-scaling failed) or temporarily block rogue IPs.
Post-incident, I'd review why auto-scaling didn't handle the load automatically.
recall: Scale out to mitigate immediate pressure

data.errorState: Code pushed to branch, no workflow appears in Actions tab
data.impact: CI/CD blocked. Code cannot be tested/deployed.

investigation.v: Check for parsing errors in the workflow file
Check 'on: push: branches' and 'paths' filters
Check if self-hosted runners are offline
Check GitHub token permissions

rca: YAML syntax is invalid OR branch/path filters exclude the commit
data.resolutionImmediate: Fix YAML syntax, adjust branch triggers
data.resolutionPerm: Use local linting tools (like 'act'), monitor runner health

practices.text: Best Practice: Keep workflow trigger logic simple
Anti-Pattern: Silently failing workflows without notifications

answer: If a workflow doesn't trigger at all, it's usually a YAML syntax error or a trigger configuration issue.
I would check the `on: push` block to ensure the branch name matches and that `paths-ignore` isn't filtering out the commit.
If using self-hosted runners, I'd verify the runner service is online and listening.
I'd validate the YAML using a linter and push a test commit to verify the fix.
recall: YAML syntax errors kill workflows silently

data.errorState: Login Failed for User / Access Denied
data.impact: App starts but fails at database connection phase.

investigation.v: Verify format (e.g., Authentication=Active Directory Default)
Check if System/User Assigned Managed Identity is enabled
Check if Identity was added as a user in the SQL DB
Check 'Allow Azure Services' or VNet rules

rca: Token rejected by SQL server (missing user mapping or firewall block)
data.resolutionImmediate: Run CREATE USER [IdentityName] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER
data.resolutionPerm: Automate SQL user creation via IaC/Deployment scripts

practices.text: Best Practice: Always use Managed Identities over passwords
Risk: Forgetting to map Identity inside the database

answer: If the network is fine but access is denied, it's an authentication issue.
I'd verify the App Service has a Managed Identity enabled and the connection string is configured to use it.
A very common miss is that the Identity exists in Azure AD, but hasn't been added as a user *inside* the SQL database.
I would connect via SSMS, run the 'CREATE USER' script for the identity, and grant it db_datareader/datawriter.
recall: Identities must be added as a user inside the SQL DB

data.reqs: Define a strategy to safely rollback failed deployments with zero/minimal downtime.
data.architecture: Detect Failure → Stop Traffic Routing → Revert to N-1 → Investigate

cost.v: Use Deployment Slots for instant swaps
Use 'kubectl rollout undo' for fast pod reversion
Never rollback DB schemas; write forward-fix migrations

answer: A robust rollback strategy relies on Blue/Green deployments. If the new version fails, we simply swap the load balancer traffic back to the old environment instantly.
For Kubernetes, I'd use `kubectl rollout undo`.
The hardest part is the database. I strictly advocate for backward-compatible schema changes.
If code rolls back, the old code must still understand the new database schema. We fix DB issues by rolling forward, not backward.

data.reqs: A developer requests prod access to troubleshoot a live issue. Balance security vs speed.
data.architecture: Request → Approval (JIT) → Time-bound Access → Revoke & Audit

cost.v: Use Privileged Identity Management for Just-In-Time access
Ensure all actions during access window are logged to Log Analytics

answer: I never grant standing 'Contributor' access to production. I follow the principle of least privilege.
For troubleshooting, I would provide them standard 'Reader' access to view logs and metrics.
If they need to execute commands or restart services, I'd use Azure PIM (Privileged Identity Management).
They request Just-In-Time (JIT) access for 2 hours, it gets approved, and every action they take is strictly audited.
recall: Use JIT / PIM for temporary elevation

title: Azure Virtual Networks: Core & Peering
definition: The fundamental building block for a secure, isolated private network environment inside Azure.
real_world_scenario: Configuring secure corporate communication lines across regional business units while ensuring zero exposure to the public internet.

architecture_flow.diagram: Spoke VNet A -> (Regional Peering) -> Central Hub -> (Global Peering) -> Spoke VNet B

core_concepts.name: Address Space
core_concepts.definition: The network's base CIDR block range.
core_concepts.usage: Allocating total allowable IP capacities (e.g., /16) to prevent exhaustion.

core_concepts.name: Subnetting
core_concepts.definition: Slicing an address space into distinct sub-networks.
core_concepts.usage: Isolating web, application, and data layers within independent blocks.

core_concepts.name: VNet Peering
core_concepts.definition: Connecting same-region networks via private paths.
core_concepts.usage: Linking spokes directly into a corporate shared-services hub network.

core_concepts.name: Global VNet Peering
core_concepts.definition: Connecting different-region networks over the backbone.
core_concepts.usage: Facilitating multi-region disaster recovery replication traffic seamlessly.

core_concepts.name: Hub-and-Spoke
core_concepts.usage: Centrally managing governance, firewalls, and gateways within the hub layout.

error_symptoms.impact: Workloads fail to communicate over the network link

investigation.command: az network vnet peering list --resource-group rg-core --vnet-name vnet-hub
investigation.purpose: Check if a matching link is created from the destination network to the source
investigation.expected_finding: Status shows Initiated instead of Connected due to missing reciprocal peering config

rca.problem: VNet Peering creation fails immediately with errors
rca.trigger: Deploying the peering resource link via IaC
rca.root_cause: The two target networks have overlapping or identical IP address space allocations
rca.impact: Cannot route packets between the defined infrastructure zones

immediate_fix: Carve out a new unique address space range block for the target network
permanent_fix: Enforce global coordination through an IP Address Management (IPAM) tool
resolution_prevention.best_practice: Map out enterprise-wide IP allocations decades in advance to safeguard against overlaps.
resolution_prevention.anti_pattern: Deploying all infrastructure instances using identical default network configurations like 10.0.0.0/16.
preventive_control: Azure Policy checks to block overlapping address blocks

response: Check routing paths via effective routes
interview_answer.why: Peering requires two completely independent, non-overlapping networks with symmetric link definitions to succeed.

interview_kill_shot: Peering routes your cross-network traffic strictly over the private Microsoft global backbone fabric; it never touches the public internet.

dynamic_cards.content: A /23 address block hosts 512 total addresses. A /25 block hosts 128 total addresses. Dividing 512 by 128 yields exactly 4 separate /25 networks.

rapid_fire_qa.question: Do you have knowledge of hub and spoke architecture?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: Yes. It is an industry standard where a central Hub network hosts shared infrastructure like firewalls, ExpressRoute gateways, and shared tooling, while isolated workloads live in Spoke networks that communicate through the Hub.

rapid_fire_qa.question: What is VNet peering? And what is the difference between VNet peering and global VNet peering?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: VNet peering joins separate networks privately. Standard peering links networks within the exact same region, whereas global peering hooks them up across entirely distinct Azure geographical zones over the private backbone.

rapid_fire_qa.question: What is the pre-requisite for VNet peering? Can we peer two VNets that have the same address space range?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: The networks must use completely non-overlapping address spaces. You can never peer networks with identical ranges because the fundamental underlying routers cannot compute ambiguous destinations.

title: Routing & Secure Endpoint Solutions
definition: Techniques used to control infrastructure traffic paths and securely expose backend systems to network workloads.
real_world_scenario: Locking down a production database so that traffic can only reach it via an internal subnet, bypassing public routing pathways entirely.

architecture_flow.diagram: App Subnet -> User Defined Route -> NSG Validation -> Private Endpoint -> Azure SQL

core_concepts.name: System Routes
core_concepts.definition: Azure's default built-in target path mappings.
core_concepts.usage: Automatically routing internal subnet components right out of the box.

core_concepts.name: User Defined Routes (UDR)
core_concepts.definition: Custom routing tables manually overriding defaults.
core_concepts.usage: Forcing all outbound cloud traffic directly through a central inspection firewall appliance.

core_concepts.name: Service Endpoints
core_concepts.definition: Subnet extensions mapping public cloud IPs safely.
core_concepts.usage: Securing a Storage target boundary over the backbone without creating private NIC interfaces.

core_concepts.name: Private Endpoints
core_concepts.definition: Private internal network interface drops for PaaS assets.
core_concepts.usage: Dropping a dedicated local IP address inside a subnet to directly represent an Azure SQL cluster.

core_concepts.name: Private Link Service
core_concepts.definition: The technology layer powering internal backend links.
core_concepts.usage: Encapsulating cross-tenant or local traffic pathways natively into safe virtual tunnels.

error_symptoms.impact: Applications cannot connect to backend storage or database environments

investigation.purpose: Verify if the target URL maps accurately to an internal IP or defaults out publicly
investigation.expected_finding: The lookup returns a public IP address because the Private DNS Zone isn't linked to the client network

rca.problem: App queries to private backends time out consistently
rca.trigger: Turning off public network flags on a targeted PaaS application database resource
rca.root_cause: The Private DNS Zone managing the database's endpoint resolution path is missing a virtual link back to the host system network

immediate_fix: Link the Private DNS Zone directly to the application network via the Portal or CLI
permanent_fix: Codify all Private DNS Zone links as mandatory components inside infrastructure templates
resolution_prevention.best_practice: Incorporate automated connectivity validation tests into pre-deployment application validation gates.
resolution_prevention.anti_pattern: Leaving public network accessibility routes wide open on production databases while using endpoints.
preventive_control: Azure Policy to completely forbid public networking configurations on data tiers

response: Validate the Private DNS Zone link state
interview_answer.why: Private endpoint setups rely on accurate internal DNS overrides to route requests cleanly to the newly created network interface.

interview_kill_shot: Service Endpoints still route to a public IP over the backbone; Private Endpoints anchor a 100% private internal network IP directly inside your client subnet.

dynamic_cards.content: Service Endpoints are cheap, light, and use public IPs at the destination resource. Private Endpoints use internal IP allocations, require careful Private DNS configuration, and fully hide resources from the public internet.

rapid_fire_qa.question: What is UDR (User Defined Route)?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: It is a custom routing table configuration that allows administrators to manually override Azure's default routing pathways, typically used to send outbound traffic through an NVA firewall.

rapid_fire_qa.question: What is a private endpoint?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: It is a network component that places a private network interface inside your subnet, mapping an internal IP directly to an Azure PaaS resource to eliminate public endpoint paths.

rapid_fire_qa.question: Can you differentiate between a service endpoint and a private endpoint?
rapid_fire_qa.kill_shot_answer: Service Endpoints extend your subnet identity to a public PaaS endpoint over the backbone. Private Endpoints pull the resource right into your subnet using an absolute private IP.

title: High Availability & Traffic Management
definition: Designing distribution systems and infrastructure nodes to withstand hardware or cloud datacenter outages gracefully.
real_world_scenario: Distributing client requests across distributed regional nodes while maintaining constant service uptime during a full cloud facility failure.

architecture_flow.diagram: Global Traffic -> Azure Front Door -> Regional App Gateway -> Multi-Zone VM Clusters

core_concepts.name: Availability Set
core_concepts.definition: Spreading virtual machines across multiple physical hardware racks.
core_concepts.usage: Protecting internal workloads from standard hardware power or patch interruptions.

core_concepts.name: Availability Zone
core_concepts.definition: Isolating systems across entirely different physical datacenters.
core_concepts.usage: Ensuring operation continues even if an entire cloud facility loses utility power.

core_concepts.name: Azure Front Door
core_concepts.definition: A global Layer 7 load balancer and CDN engine.
core_concepts.usage: Routing internet users to the lowest-latency regional entry node via Anycast protocols.

core_concepts.name: Application Gateway
core_concepts.definition: A regional Layer 7 load balancer with advanced rules.
core_concepts.usage: Managing cookie-based sticky routing paths and internal URL-based resource mappings.

core_concepts.name: Fault Domain
core_concepts.definition: A hardware grouping that shares a common power source.
core_concepts.usage: Ensuring multiple compute nodes do not rely on the same power strip or switch infrastructure.

error_symptoms.impact: Users hit generic error screens when making secure web requests

investigation.command: az network application-gateway backend-health show -g rg-prod -n app-gw
investigation.purpose: Identify if ingress routers are actively receiving signals from the behind-the-scenes clusters
investigation.expected_finding: Probes report Unhealthy due to application runtime failures on specific nodes

rca.problem: Traffic distributions break intermittently under heavy query load patterns
rca.trigger: An underlying hardware host asset encounters sudden failure conditions
